title: 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple
review:
Zombie horror can offer plenty of brutality. Finding something beautiful inside it is harder. The Bone Temple does both, delivering a continuation that feels unpredictable, disturbing, and surprisingly full of life.

Two stories unfold and collide without feeling like another familiar trip through the same world. There are moments when the characters become so absorbing that you almost forget you’re watching a zombie movie. Then something deeply unsettling happens, or something makes you laugh, and you remember how strange this whole experience is. Hilarious and disturbing is a difficult combination to pull off. This one gets there.

Ralph Fiennes is the standout. The doctor’s connection with Samson gives the film an unexpected tenderness, making room for something beyond the threat of another monster. Those scenes were among the most compelling parts of the movie—strange, beautiful, and genuinely exciting to watch.

The connection between the younger characters gives the chaos another emotional anchor. There’s something worth caring about in how they find each other and offer protection inside such an ugly world. Add the gorgeous cinematography, striking shots, and an ending that leaves you buzzing, and the whole thing feels alive with possibility.

Holy fuck, this was a fantastic surprise. It left us wanting to watch it again and excited to see where this world goes next.

title: Dead Man’s Wire
review:
Dead Man’s Wire finds an entertaining rhythm inside a serious situation. The tension is there, but so are moments of playfulness and unexpected relaxation. The music carries a lot of that contrast, giving a movie built around one hostage standoff more personality than the setup might suggest.

The lead performance keeps it compelling. There’s something interesting about watching someone who feels unstable without seeming eager to become a killer. That uncertainty makes him sympathetic enough to follow, even as the situation gets further out of hand.

The radio DJ is another standout, and the reporter’s storyline adds welcome depth beyond the immediate confrontation. Those different angles help keep the movie engaging. It never became boring, but they also hint at how much more there might have been to explore.

That’s the main frustration: the film stays so close to the standoff that the life surrounding it can feel just out of reach. More of what brought him there—how he felt screwed over, pieces of his past, another perspective—could have given the story greater range. Staying tightly focused is an interesting choice; it just leaves you wanting another layer.

The real footage afterward makes the portrayal feel especially convincing. It’s an unbelievable story, carried by strong performances and a soundtrack that knows how to play against the tension. An enjoyable watch, with enough going for it to make you wish it had opened its world a little wider.

title: The Choral
review:
There’s something quietly sad about people building a life together while a war keeps pulling it apart. The Choral finds beauty, humor, and warmth in that space, following a group whose shared purpose becomes harder to hold onto as the world changes around them.

The pleasure is often in the people. The central character’s personality and the way he runs things give the film energy, while the younger characters and those connected to the army bring entertaining moments of their own. The bikes, outfits, and sets make the period setting enjoyable to spend time in, with different lives unfolding around the choir.

Watching the group improve gives the story a satisfying progression. The singing can be beautiful, and it avoids the cheesiness that sometimes makes musicals difficult to settle into. But those performances also slow the film down. There’s a lot to appreciate without every musical stretch being equally absorbing, and the running time starts to make itself felt.

What gives the movie weight is the gradual loss of the people bringing those voices together. The story comes full circle in a way that feels sad rather than reassuring. People try to be patriotic and keep something meaningful alive, while having very little say in what happens to them.

That feeling—being a pawn in a much bigger game—lingers beyond the music. A worthwhile watch with heartfelt and funny moments, even if its slower passages keep it from landing more strongly.

title: No Other Choice
review:
Providing for your family sounds like a reason almost anyone can understand. No Other Choice takes that instinct somewhere deeply uncomfortable, making you root for a man while questioning how much you’re willing to excuse just because you understand what he wants.

It’s funny, absorbing, and full of interesting characters. The situations keep unfolding in ways that make it easy to follow someone who is clearly getting in over his head. Even the length feels earned. There wasn’t a stretch that seemed disposable, and the story flows well enough that the subtitles become part of the experience rather than an obstacle.

A little more time inside some of the other characters’ lives would have been welcome. There’s plenty happening around this man’s pursuit, and those glimpses are interesting enough to leave you curious. Still, the movie keeps its focus and holds your attention.

The uncomfortable part is how familiar his sense of desperation can feel. Sometimes wanting something badly enough makes every alternative seem impossible. You stop asking whether the goal is worth it and start treating anything in the way as something to overcome. But if getting there means making everyone around you suffer, maybe what needs to change is the thing you’re chasing.

That’s the bitter pill. The movie makes his pursuit entertaining without making it easy to feel good about. You can understand the pressure, enjoy the humor, and still find yourself thinking: hold on, what the fuck am I rooting for?

A really good film that keeps you engaged in the moment and leaves the harder questions waiting afterward.

title: Night Patrol
review:
Night Patrol looks like it’s heading down a familiar road: cops, gang violence, and a situation you can already imagine ending badly. Then it takes a turn that makes the whole thing more playful—and more entertaining—than the trailer suggested.

That surprise does a lot for the movie. There’s real-world ugliness underneath the setup, but the film twists it into something stranger, keeping you guessing about what might happen next. Going in expecting a straightforward cop movie makes that change of direction especially enjoyable.

The pacing doesn’t always keep up with the chaos. Some stretches drag, and the cheesiness can be hard to miss. Still, the performances bring enough fun and playfulness to keep it from becoming a dull watch. It has slow parts without losing all its energy.

Justin Long’s character is harder to get a read on. He seems positioned as a good cop while continuing to do shady shit, and the movie doesn’t always make that contradiction convincing. Is he conflicted? Trying to do better? Just another bad guy? There’s room for that uncertainty to be interesting, but here it can feel more confusing than compelling.

What carries Night Patrol is its willingness to take the familiar setup somewhere unexpected. Messy in places, uneven in its momentum, but entertaining enough to make the surprise worthwhile. More fun than expected, even when it doesn’t quite make sense.

title: The Fire Raven
review:
The Fire Raven packs action, mystery, thriller tension, and some nasty violence into a story that keeps you busy figuring out who’s who and what the hell is happening. It’s creative, occasionally goofy, and a little cheesy—but there’s enough going on to make the ride entertaining.

The brother-and-sister relationship gives that chaos something to hold onto. Beneath the shifting suspicions and competing storylines, the family connections are what make the movie land. The emotional weight becomes clearer as the pieces come together, giving the mystery more than just another answer to chase.

Following those pieces can take some work. With so much happening onscreen, reading the subtitles sometimes means missing a look, a detail, or part of the action. The broad strokes are easy enough to follow, but keeping track of everyone’s role can feel like playing catch-up. By the end, earlier moments start clicking into place.

There’s fun in trying to get ahead of it, too. After enough mysteries, you start recognizing when a movie is steering you toward someone suspicious. You think you’ve caught the trick—until it sends you somewhere else. That guessing game helps keep this one engaging.

The ending stretches that patience a little. It reaches what feels like a stopping point, then adds another piece, then another. Those extra beats help bring things together, but they also make the finish feel drawn out. And the gore can be a bit much, even when the action is otherwise enjoyable.

Still, the family story gives the spectacle a feeling that lasts beyond the mystery. Uneven, busy, and sometimes exhausting, but a good watch with an emotional payoff underneath all the moving parts.

title: Clika
review:
Clika finds its appeal in a dream that feels close to home: making music with your friends, building something for your family, and trying to turn what you love into a future. The struggles along the way give that ambition weight, but the movie keeps the experience fun and entertaining from beginning to end.

There’s a particular pleasure in seeing California communities and familiar places represented onscreen. The setting feels recognizable, and the Latin culture is a big part of what makes the film connect. You’re watching people pursue something meaningful in a world you can recognize, which makes it easier to get invested in where they’re headed.

The music, friendships, and family ties give that pursuit its appeal. Chasing a dream involves the people beside you as much as the person trying to make it happen, and that shared experience is what makes this an enjoyable watch.

The acting is uneven. Some characters feel less convincing than others, and those weaker performances stand out. Fortunately, the stronger ones do enough to carry the film through those moments without losing the connection that makes it work.

Clika leaves a good feeling. An entertaining story about ambition and the people you bring along with you, with a welcome sense of recognition for the culture and communities it puts onscreen.

title: Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die
review:
Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die takes our relationship with technology to a ridiculous extreme, but the uncomfortable part is how much already feels familiar. The phones, the escape into virtual worlds, the promise of AI—it’s a satirical nightmare with enough truth underneath the chaos to make the jokes sting.

It’s also really fucking entertaining. The characters are interesting, the lead is easy to root for, and the story keeps finding ways to catch you off guard. For a movie dealing with such bleak possibilities, it has enough humor and unpredictability to keep the experience playful rather than crushing.

The technology itself isn’t the whole problem. There’s something exciting about tools that could connect people or open experiences they couldn’t otherwise access. The ugliness comes from what happens when those possibilities find a different purpose. Somewhere between convenience and escape, the question becomes: what are we giving up, and what are we so desperate to get away from?

That’s where it starts feeling like a modern-day Idiocracy. You laugh at the exaggeration, recognize pieces of your own world, then leave the theater and reach for your phone. The movie can point at the problem, but recognizing yourself in the joke doesn’t necessarily change anything. That’s a weird feeling to carry out of something this fun.

Not every piece lands. Some of the group gets much more attention than the rest, leaving other characters feeling less explored. The later stretch also pushes the silliness and drama further than it needs to. Still, the likable lead, surprising turns, and jokes worth catching keep it engaging.

Funny, strange, and full of ideas—an entertaining watch with an uncomfortable thought underneath it: we might already be living inside part of the punchline.

title: Whistle
review:
Whistle takes the classic “don’t touch that” horror setup and gives it a nasty hook: an ancient death whistle whose sound brings your future death looking for you. Curiosity gets the story moving. Figuring out how to survive the consequences is another problem entirely.

There’s something unsettling about that idea. Death isn’t a stranger picking victims at random—it’s something that already belongs to you, arriving before you’re ready. The threat turns the future into something immediate, making the question less about who’s coming and more about whether there’s any way to escape what’s yours.

The high-school setting adds a familiar pressure to the supernatural setup. A group of young people has to make sense of something far beyond their experience, with every unanswered question carrying a potentially ugly consequence. It’s a straightforward horror engine with a hook that doesn’t need much explaining.

The appeal is in that simplicity: a cursed object, a terrible sound, and the desperate search for a way to take back what’s been set in motion. Sometimes the scariest part of a bad decision is realizing that understanding it came too late.

title: Melania
review:
Melania follows the twenty days leading up to the 2025 presidential inauguration, but our biggest takeaway was how bizarre the whole experience felt. It’s a trippy watch—not because it’s a fantasy, but because this is an actual person’s life unfolding around an enormous public event.

There’s curiosity in that. You’re watching a world most people will never experience, and that alone gives you something to take in. But finding something interesting isn’t the same as loving the movie built around it. That’s where this landed for us: curious about what we were watching, without coming away particularly impressed.

The strangeness is what sticks. It’s a film we’d describe as an experience more readily than a recommendation—something that held our curiosity, but didn’t turn that curiosity into a stronger connection.
